overview: This imported label covers East African coastal towns, especially the Swahili trading world, rather than every Islamic city or one united empire. African settlements developed into connected centres with distinct rulers and communities. The map’s 1000 to 1650 window is a broad regional selection; individual towns began and changed at different times.

periods.title: Expanding coastal connections
periods.summary: African coastal settlements participated in Indian Ocean routes; navigation, ports and urban architecture developed over many centuries.

periods.title: Kilwa and neighbouring towns
periods.summary: Kilwa prospered in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries; monumental mosques, houses and palaces expressed its wealth.

periods.title: Different towns, different fortunes
periods.summary: Portuguese intervention affected Kilwa in the sixteenth century, while Gedi remained part of coastal urban history into the seventeenth.

items.text: These towns belonged to a sailing network. Medieval Yemeni records describe ships travelling from Mogadishu to Arabian ports, while a vessel from Kilwa reached Aden with rice in 1336. Merchants moved food, cloth, ivory and other goods; the same routes also carried enslaved people.

At Kilwa, gold and ivory from the African interior could be exchanged for Persian ceramics, Chinese porcelain, silver and perfumes. Coastal prosperity therefore depended on inland producers and routes as well as ships arriving over the horizon.

Kilwa’s Great Mosque combined coral stone and lime mortar with domes and vaults. Some vaults contained imported Chinese porcelain as decoration: an overseas bowl could become part of a building rather than remain on a dinner table.

Husuni Kubwa, built around 1310 to 1333, included a large eight-sided bathing pool. The surviving palace makes elite comfort unusually visible, although a ruler’s pool tells us much more about wealthy residents than ordinary household washing.

At Songo Mnara, charred seeds reveal a varied pantry: pearl millet, finger millet, sorghum, rice, beans, coconut and fruits such as baobab. Studying the tiny burnt leftovers helps recover meals that disappeared centuries before anyone could write down their recipes.

Fish bones are plentiful at Songo Mnara, but they are not a simple menu chart. Chemical analysis of seven people’s bones suggested that certain grains and cattle or chicken contributed more to their diets than marine foods. Archaeologists compare different clues because a heap of bones can be misleading.

House 44 doubled as a workplace. Spindle whorls, the small weights used when spinning thread, occurred in every room, showing that cotton production was woven into household life. Cooking and manufacturing shared space: no separate office commute required.

Stone houses were only part of the town. Excavations at Songo Mnara also uncovered earth-and-daub homes whose residents used imported pottery, ornaments and coins. A building’s material alone cannot tell us whether its occupants were poor.

In Songo Mnara’s houses, mangrove beams supported roofs, and small wall recesses held oil lamps. Bright white walls once carried fabric hangings. The building commonly labelled the Palace is interpreted by the community research project as a particularly grand merchant’s home.

Benches beside doorways provided places for relatives and friends to sit and talk. That small architectural detail gives the ruined streets a social soundtrack: conversation belonged at the threshold between a home and the wider town.

Gedi stood about 6.5 kilometres inland, yet participated in ocean trade. Its two enclosing walls separated a monumental centre from more modest houses used by most residents. Imported luxury objects reveal connections and wealth, but its commerce also included the export of enslaved people.

Gedi’s builders provided wells, stone water conduits, storage jars and tanks. Surviving houses include bathrooms and toilets, while sumps drained rainwater from courtyards and streets. Keeping a crowded town supplied and drained required practical engineering as well as impressive monuments.

A copper coin issued at Kilwa around 1320 to 1335 preserves the Arabic words يثق بالواحد المنان, translated by the Ashmolean Museum as “Trust in the One (God), the Bountiful.” Its other side names al-Hasan ibn Sulayman. This is an Arabic coin inscription, not a specimen of written Swahili.

ending.text: There was no single fall of these towns in 1650. Gedi was eventually abandoned, while coastal communities continued. Songo Mnara remains a lived-in island whose residents help interpret and care for its heritage.
